# 2 Maccabees Chapter 13 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic Equivalence)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 2 Maccabees 13 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/2MA_013_page_001.jpg

---

**13:1** In the 149th year, word reached Judas and his men: Antiochus Eupator was marching on Judea with a massive force.

**13:2** With him was Lysias, his guardian and chief minister. Each of them commanded a Greek force of 110,000 infantry, 5,300 cavalry, 22 elephants, and 300 scythed chariots.

**13:3** Menelaus had joined them too, flattering Antiochus and urging him forward — not out of any concern for his country, but hoping this would help him hold onto power.

**13:4** But the King of kings turned Antiochus's fury against the traitor. When Lysias made it clear that Menelaus was behind all the trouble, Antiochus ordered him taken to Beroea and executed in the way that city executes people.

**13:5** There is a tower in Beroea fifty cubits high, filled with ashes. It has a rim running around it that slopes sharply inward over the ashes on all sides.

**13:6** Whoever is guilty of sacrilege or other notorious crimes is shoved into the tower and pushed to their death in the ashes below.

**13:7** That is how Menelaus the lawbreaker died — not even receiving a proper burial in the ground.

**13:8** Fitting, really. He had committed so many sins against the altar — the altar whose fire and ashes were holy — that he died in ashes.

**13:9** The king came on in a savage mood, planning to make the Jews suffer far worse than they had under his father.

**13:10** Judas heard about it and ordered the people to cry out to the Lord day and night — now more than ever, they needed God to help those who were about to lose their law, their homeland, and the holy temple.

**13:11** He did not want this people — who had only just begun to recover — to fall again into the hands of godless pagans.

**13:12** For three days the whole community lay face down on the ground, weeping and fasting without stop, begging the merciful God for help. Then Judas urged them to their feet and ordered them to make ready.

**13:13** After consulting privately with the elders, he decided to strike before the king's army could enter Judea and take the city. They would trust God to decide the outcome.

**13:14** He committed the decision to the Creator of the world and urged his men to fight bravely to the death for the law, the temple, the city, their homeland, and their way of life. He set up camp near Modein.

**13:15** He gave his men the watchword: "God's victory." He then picked the best young fighters he had and led a night raid on the royal tent. They killed around two thousand men in the camp and ran a sword through the lead elephant and its rider.

**13:16** In the end they left the entire camp in a state of panic and confusion, and they pulled back triumphant.

**13:17** All this happened just as day was breaking, because the Lord's protection was over him.

**13:18** The king, getting a feel now for how bold the Jews could be, tried a different approach and attempted to take their positions by trickery.

**13:19** He marched against Beth-zur, a strong Jewish fortress. He was repulsed, failed, and took losses.

**13:20** Maccabeus got supplies through to the garrison inside.

**13:21** But a man named Rhodocus from within the Jewish ranks leaked secret information to the enemy. He was tracked down, arrested, and locked up.

**13:22** The king opened talks with Beth-zur again, shook hands on an agreement, received their pledge in return, and withdrew.

**13:23** He attacked Judas and was beaten back. Then news came that Philip — whom he had left in charge at Antioch — had staged a revolt. He was shaken. He offered the Jews terms, accepted all fair conditions, swore an oath, and left. He made sacrifice to the Lord, honored the temple, treated Maccabeus generously, and departed.

**13:24** He appointed Hegemonides as governor from Ptolemais down to Gerra.

**13:25** When he went to Ptolemais, the locals were furious about the peace treaty — they wanted it canceled.

**13:26** Lysias got up on the platform and put forward the best case he could. He won them over, talked them down, and secured their cooperation. Then he returned to Antioch. That was how the king's campaign ended.
